title: Citation Rules: When a Citation Is Required
body:
A citation is required whenever a record states a fact it did not itself establish: a number taken from a public dataset, a quotation from a public-domain work, a standard's requirement, a public record's contents. A citation is not required for the database's own original work — a Signature design, a generated variation, a computed demo result — because the record itself is the source, and it says so in its provenance field.

The test is simple: could a reader reasonably ask "where did that come from?" If yes, the answer belongs in the record, as a citation, not as a vague gesture toward "the internet" or "public knowledge." A fact without a citable public source is not stated as fact here; it is labeled as designed, estimated, or unproven, according to what the evidence actually supports.
demo_code:
cases={'Number from a public dataset':'CITE','Quotation from a public-domain work':'CITE','A standard requirement':'CITE','Own original design':'Record itself is the source','Computed demo result':'Demo code is the source'}
for k,v in cases.items(): print(f'{k} -> {v}')
demo_output:
Number from a public dataset -> CITE
Quotation from a public-domain work -> CITE
A standard requirement -> CITE
Own original design -> Record itself is the source
Computed demo result -> Demo code is the source
provenance: Signature citation guidance; Signature works cite public sources and label completions as Signature.

title: Citation Rules: What Counts as a Public Source
body:
A public source is a source anyone can inspect without private access, private membership, or personal data: government publications and datasets, public records, published standards, public-domain works, and openly published reference works. The source must be identifiable — a title, a publisher or agency, and a date or edition — so a reader can find the same source and check the same passage.

What does not count: private communications, paywalled material quoted without access, personal data, and social-media posts. This database never cites Facebook or any private platform, and never cites a source the reader cannot inspect. A claim whose only support is a private source is not published as fact; it waits until a public source exists, or it is labeled as designed.
demo_output:
PUBLIC: Government publications
PUBLIC: Public records
PUBLIC: Published standards
PUBLIC: Public-domain works
PUBLIC: Open reference works
NEVER CITED: private communications, personal data, social-media posts
provenance: Signature citation guidance; Signature works cite public sources and label completions as Signature.

title: Format: Government Data and Datasets
body:
Format for government data: Agency. Dataset or publication title. Edition or version. Date. Access point (the agency's own site or data portal). Example, stated as a format example rather than a claim about any single table: U.S. Census Bureau. American Community Survey, 1-year estimates. 2024. Data available through the Census Bureau's data portal. The agency comes first because the agency is the guarantor; the date comes last in the citation because datasets are revised, and a citation without a vintage can silently point at a different table.

Rule: cite the dataset, not the search engine that found it, and cite the vintage you actually used. If a dataset is revised after you cite it, the citation still points at the vintage named, which is exactly why the vintage is part of the citation.
demo_code:
print('U.S. Census Bureau. American Community Survey, 1-year estimates. 2024.')
print('Rule: agency first (the guarantor), vintage named (datasets are revised).')
demo_output:
U.S. Census Bureau. American Community Survey, 1-year estimates. 2024.
Rule: agency first (the guarantor), vintage named (datasets are revised).
provenance: Signature citation guidance; Signature works cite public sources and label completions as Signature.

title: Format: Public Records and Patent Records
body:
Format for public records: Issuing office. Record title or description. Record identifier, where one exists. Date. Example, at collection level: United States Patent and Trademark Office. Patent Full-Text Database. Public patent records as published by the Office. A single patent, when cited, is cited by its number and title exactly as the Office prints them — never from memory, never rounded, never guessed.

Rule: a patent record proves that a claim was made and published, not that the invention works. Citations in this network keep that distinction in the sentence around the citation, not just in the citation itself, so a reader never mistakes "patented" for "proven to work."
demo_code:
print('United States Patent and Trademark Office. Patent Full-Text Database.')
print('Single patent: number + title exactly as the Office prints them.')
print('Rule: patented proves a claim was published, not that it works.')
demo_output:
United States Patent and Trademark Office. Patent Full-Text Database.
Single patent: number + title exactly as the Office prints them.
Rule: patented proves a claim was published, not that it works.
provenance: Signature citation guidance; Signature works cite public sources and label completions as Signature.

title: Format: Standards
body:
Format for standards: Standards body. Standard title. Designation and edition. Date. Example, at body level: National Institute of Standards and Technology. Standards and measurements publications as issued by the Institute. When a specific standard is cited, its full designation and edition are given, because a standard's requirements change between editions and a citation to "the standard" without an edition is ambiguous.

Rule: cite the edition you followed, and state in the record whether compliance is claimed or the standard is merely referenced. Referencing a standard is not the same as meeting it, and this network never lets a reference borrow the authority of a compliance claim.
demo_code:
print('National Institute of Standards and Technology. Standards publications, as issued.')
print('Specific standard: full designation + edition + date.')
print('Rule: referencing a standard is not claiming compliance with it.')
demo_output:
National Institute of Standards and Technology. Standards publications, as issued.
Specific standard: full designation + edition + date.
Rule: referencing a standard is not claiming compliance with it.
provenance: Signature citation guidance; Signature works cite public sources and label completions as Signature.

title: Format: Public-Domain Works
body:
Format for public-domain works: Author. Title. Original publication date. Public-domain source edition. Example, fully real: Jane Austen. Pride and Prejudice. 1813. Project Gutenberg edition. A public-domain work is cited to its original publication first, because the work's date is part of its identity, and to the source edition second, so the reader can find the same text.

Rule: public-domain status is a legal fact about a specific work, not a general property of old books. This network cites a work as public-domain only where that status is established for that work, and it never reproduces copyrighted text under a public-domain label. When in doubt, the work is described, not quoted.
demo_code:
print('Jane Austen. Pride and Prejudice. 1813. Project Gutenberg edition.')
print('Rule: original date first, source edition second.')
print('Public-domain status is per-work, never assumed.')
demo_output:
Jane Austen. Pride and Prejudice. 1813. Project Gutenberg edition.
Rule: original date first, source edition second.
Public-domain status is per-work, never assumed.
provenance: Signature citation guidance; Signature works cite public sources and label completions as Signature.

title: Sample Citations Across Subjects
body:
Across subjects, the same discipline holds. Science: cite the dataset and its vintage, as in the government-data format. Law and public records: cite the issuing office and the record exactly as issued. Technology: cite the standard with its designation and edition. Literature: cite the author, the original date, and the public-domain edition. History: cite the archive and the item, with its date, so a later reader can sit in front of the same document.

A sample citation is only a sample until it is used: when a database record leans on one of these sources, the citation moves into that record's provenance, with the passage or table named. A citations database that only lists formats without ever attaching them to claims is a style guide; this one exists to be used, record by record.
demo_code:
samples={'Science':'dataset + vintage','Law / public records':'issuing office + record as issued','Technology':'standard designation + edition','Literature':'author + original date + edition','History':'archive + item + date'}
for k,v in samples.items(): print(f'{k}: {v}')
demo_output:
Science: dataset + vintage
Law / public records: issuing office + record as issued
Technology: standard designation + edition
Literature: author + original date + edition
History: archive + item + date

title: The Citation Index: How to Find a Citation Again
body:
The citation index is organized by source type first — government data, public records, standards, public-domain works — then by subject, then by date. A reader looking for the source of a number starts from the record that states it, follows its provenance to the citation, and finds the citation in the index under its source type. No citation lives only in prose: every citation used by a record is also an entry here, with its full format, so the index and the records cannot drift apart silently.

Maintenance rule: when a source is revised, the index gains a new entry for the new vintage; the old entry is never overwritten, because old records cite the old vintage. An index that rewrites history destroys the very checking it exists to enable.
demo_output:
Index section: Government data (then subject, then date)
Index section: Public records (then subject, then date)
Index section: Standards (then subject, then date)
Index section: Public-domain works (then subject, then date)
Rule: revisions add entries; old entries are never overwritten.
provenance: Signature citation guidance; Signature works cite public sources and label completions as Signature.

title: Citing Signature Works and Completions
body:
A Signature work cites its public sources the same way any work does, and then adds one more line: what is Signature-made. A Signature completion of a public record states the public source it completes, what was missing, and what was created to complete it, labeled Signature. The label is not decoration; it is the boundary between "this is public record" and "this was made to complete it," and removing it would mislead every later reader.

Rule: a Signature work never cites itself as a public source, never presents a generated completion as a harvested record, and never borrows a public source's authority for its invented parts. The public parts carry public citations; the Signature parts carry the Signature label; the seam between them is visible in the record.
demo_code:
print('Signature work citation = public citations + one more line:')
print('  what is Signature-made, and where the seam is.')
print('Rule: never cite a Signature work as a public source.')
demo_output:
Signature work citation = public citations + one more line:
  what is Signature-made, and where the seam is.
Rule: never cite a Signature work as a public source.
provenance: Signature citation guidance; Signature works cite public sources and label completions as Signature.

title: What This Database Refuses to Cite
body:
This database refuses four things, plainly. One: private sources presented as public evidence. Two: social-media posts, including Facebook, as sources for facts — a post may inspire a question, but it never answers one here. Three: sources the reader cannot inspect. Four: citations invented to dress up a claim — a citation must point at a source that was actually consulted, and a fabricated citation is worse than none, because it borrows trust it did not earn.

A record that cannot be cited to a public source is not hidden; it is labeled for what it is — designed, estimated, generated, or unproven — and published with that label intact. Refusing a false citation is not a gap in the database. It is the database working.
demo_output:
REFUSED: Private sources as public evidence
REFUSED: Social-media posts as fact sources
REFUSED: Sources the reader cannot inspect
REFUSED: Fabricated citations
Instead: label the record designed, estimated, generated, or unproven.
